passage: Kunal's phone lit up: 'okay.' Just that, lowercase, with a full stop. He stared at it. Samir was usually all capital letters and exclamation marks. A full stop felt like a closed door. Kunal wrote back, 'you good?' Two minutes later, 'OKAY!!! sorry, was in the middle of football and my hands were muddy.' Kunal grinned and typed, 'sooooo you're not angry?' Samir sent, 'Lol no, I was just typing with one thumb.' Kunal put the phone away, half laughing at himself. On the walk to school he said, "Your full stops are scary, you know." Samir shrugged. "They're just how I type when I'm rushed." They agreed to ask when in doubt.

qa.q: What was Samir's first message?
qa.a: It was 'okay.' in lowercase with a full stop.

qa.q: Why did Kunal write 'you good?' after the first message?
qa.a: The lowercase word with a full stop felt cold to him, and he worried Samir might be upset. He could not tell the mood without checking.

qa.q: What could Kunal do when a short message feels cold?
qa.a: Ask a light question like 'you good?', because punctuation suggests a mood but does not prove it.

qa.q: How might Samir have seen Samir's own message?
qa.a: As an ordinary quick reply typed with one thumb, with no cold meaning. 🙂

grounding: Punctuation and capitalisation are read for mood in text, but they suggest and do not prove.

passage:
"Look at this," said Swati, holding out her phone. "She wrote 'fine.' Full stop. She never uses full stops."
"So?" said Yogesh.
"So she's angry."
"Or she's busy. Or her keyboard's odd." He scrolled up. "Here she wrote 'sooooo excited!!!' last night. That's her being playful, not her being loud."
"It's just confusing. Some of my friends use capitals to shout and some to be happy."
"Then you can't tell from the letters," said Yogesh. "You'd have to ask."
Swati sighed and typed, 'you okay? your fine sounded serious.' The reply came fast: 'haha sorry, I was in the middle of a test. I'm fine!'

qa.q: What did Swati's friend write?
qa.a: She wrote 'fine.' with a full stop.

qa.q: Why did Swati think her friend was angry?
qa.a: She noticed the full stop, which the friend never used, and read it as a sign of cold or angry mood. Yogesh pointed out other explanations such as being busy or a keyboard quirk.

qa.q: What could Swati try instead of guessing?
qa.a: Ask the friend directly if she is okay, as she did.

qa.q: How might the friend feel when she reads Swati's question?
qa.a: She may feel cared for and amused, since she was just in the middle of a test.

grounding: Punctuation and capitalisation suggest a mood but do not prove it, and asking is wiser.

passage:
When I invited Akash to my birthday lunch, his reply was just: "okay."
With a full stop. No emoji. I spent the whole evening decoding it. In my friend group, "okay." with a full stop means you're annoyed. Like, "fine, whatever."
Next day I asked him carefully, "Are you upset about something? Your okay seemed cold."
He looked totally lost. "Cold? I always use full stops. My dad's an English teacher. He'd die if I didn't."
I laughed so hard. I scrolled up our chat. He'd written "okay." to literally everything, including "I got you a samosa."
So now I know: my group reads a full stop as cold. His family reads no full stop as lazy. Same dot, two meanings.
He came to the lunch. He brought a card. It said: "Happy birthday. See you soon." Full stops everywhere.
- Kiran

qa.q: What was Akash's reply to the invitation?
qa.a: Just "okay." with a full stop.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while decoding the reply?
qa.a: Kiran felt anxious and hurt, worrying that the full stop meant Akash was annoyed.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that cleared up the confusion?
qa.a: Kiran asked Akash directly and gently instead of assuming, which revealed the full stop was just his habit.

qa.q: How does Akash's family see full stops compared with Kiran's friends?
qa.a: Akash's family sees them as correct and polite, while Kiran's friend group reads them as cold.

grounding: The account shows a full stop being read as cold in one group and normal in another, so punctuation suggests but does not prove a mood.

passage:
Counsellor's note - Kashish, Class 9, Monday
Nirmala came to see me at break, upset. She said her mother had been angry with her all weekend. When I asked why she thought so, she showed me the texts: "COME HOME BY 6." "DID YOU EAT?" "CALL ME WHEN YOU REACH."
All in capitals. Nirmala said, "She's shouting at me in every message."
I asked if her mother had sounded angry on the phone. Nirmala thought and said, "No. Normal. She asked about my test."
We looked at the messages again together. No harsh words, only capital letters. I wondered aloud if her mother simply types that way, perhaps with caps lock on, or because it's easier to read.
Nirmala laughed for the first time. "She does hold the phone very far away."
She agreed to ask her mother that evening. Tuesday she told me: caps lock, stuck for a year.

qa.q: What did one of the mother's texts say?
qa.a: "COME HOME BY 6."

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she came to see Kashish?
qa.a: Nirmala felt upset and anxious, believing her mother was shouting at her in every message.

qa.q: How did Kashish help Nirmala read the messages differently?
qa.a: Kashish asked how her mother sounded on the phone and looked at the words with her, suggesting other reasons for capitals before assuming anger.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's mother feel if she learned her caps looked like shouting?
qa.a: She would probably feel surprised and sorry, since she was only checking on her daughter.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows capital letters read as shouting, and the reader learning such cues suggest but don't prove a mood.

passage:
Thursday
Asif sent me this after I told him about the science fair: "OKAY!!! that is sooooo cool"
First I was thrilled. Then I started wondering. OKAY with three exclamation marks. Is he shouting? Is "sooooo" sarcastic? My brother says long vowels mean someone's making fun of you.
But Asif doesn't really do sarcasm. And he'd been asking about the project all week. And his last message had a party emoji.
So maybe it was just... excitement.
I didn't want to guess forever, so I texted: "haha was that real excitement or sarcastic excitement?"
He replied: "REAL. why would I be sarcastic?? can I come see it?"
My brother reads it one way, Asif writes it another. I'm learning to look at the person, not just the letters.
- Indu

qa.q: What did Asif's message say?
qa.a: "OKAY!!! that is sooooo cool"

qa.q: What was Indu feeling after reading the message?
qa.a: Indu felt thrilled at first, then unsure and a little worried that the capitals and long vowels might be sarcastic.

qa.q: What small step helped Indu stop guessing?
qa.a: Asking lightly whether it was real or sarcastic excitement, and looking at Asif's usual style and earlier messages.

qa.q: How does Indu's brother read long vowels compared with Asif?
qa.a: Indu's brother reads them as mocking, while Asif uses them to show excitement.

grounding: The diary shows capitals, exclamation marks and repeated letters suggesting but not proving a mood, and norms differing between people.

passage:

Pradeep: okay.
Urmila: ...okay with a full stop? are you annoyed? 😬
Pradeep: no?? why
Urmila: in my group a full stop at the end is basically a door slam
Pradeep: lol I put full stops on everything. my dad taught me to text like I'm writing a letter
Urmila: ahh. that explains the "Good morning." every single day
Pradeep: exactly. if I'm ever annoyed you'll know, I'll write a whole paragraph
Urmila: noted. ok so friday is yours
Pradeep: OKAY!!! better?
Urmila: sooooo much better 😄
Pradeep: good. and thank you. monday was going to be a mess for me

qa.q: Which day did Urmila offer to take instead?
qa.a: Urmila offered to take Monday instead.

qa.q: What was Urmila worried about on seeing 'okay.'?
qa.a: Urmila was worried that Pradeep was annoyed, since in Urmila's group a full stop feels like a door slam; it could just as well have been a habit, which it turned out to be.

qa.q: Why was asking directly the right move?
qa.a: Punctuation only suggests a mood and norms differ, so asking cleared up that the full stops were a letter-writing habit, not coldness.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see a full stop?
qa.a: For Pradeep a full stop is just normal punctuation, taught by Pradeep's dad; real annoyance would come as a whole paragraph.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a full stop as cold and capitals and repeated letters as excitement, while learning such cues differ from person to person.
